docs.title: pyheclib
docs.text:
Read and write HEC-DSS files from Python.

HEC-DSS is the database format used by HEC-HMS, HEC-RAS and other tools from the US Army Corps of Engineers' Hydrologic Engineering Center. pyheclib works with DSS version 7 files and gives you the data as numpy arrays and pandas objects.

docs.title: What you can store
docs.text: Record type Use it for Page RegularTs time series with a fixed interval, like hourly flow Regular time series IrregularTs time series with any timing, like field readings Irregular time series PairedData curves, like rating or storage tables Paired data GriddedData rasters, like radar rainfall or a DEM Gridded data

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install pyheclib

Works on Python 3.8 or newer. Prebuilt packages are available for:

  • Linux (x86_64)
  • macOS (Apple Silicon, macOS 14 or newer)
  • Windows (64 bit)

Note

DSS version 6 files are not supported. Open them in HEC-DSSVue and save them as version 7 first.

docs.title: A short example
docs.text:
import pyheclib as phl

with phl.open("example.dss") as dss_file:
    flow = phl.RegularTs("/BASIN/GAGE/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/", values=[10.0, 12.5, 15.0],
                         start="2020-01-01 01:00", unit="CFS")
    dss_file.write(flow)

    record = dss_file.read("/BASIN/GAGE/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/")
    print(record.to_series())

Next, read Getting started to learn how files and pathnames work.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Everything you can use from pyheclib, with a short description of each class and function. The record type pages have longer examples.

import pyheclib as phl
Name What it is open open or create a DSS file DssFile an open DSS file, used to write, read, list and delete records RegularTs regular time series record IrregularTs irregular time series record PairedData paired data (curves) record GriddedData gridded data (raster) record DssPath a DSS pathname split into its six parts set_message_level set how much the HEC-DSS library logs message_level_from_env read the log level from DSS_MESSAGE_LEVEL api_version version of the bundled HEC-DSS library

docs.title: open
docs.text:
phl.open(filename) -> DssFile

Opens a DSS version 7 file. If the file does not exist, it is created. Returns a DssFile.

Parameter Type Description filename str path of the .dss file 
dss_file = phl.open("example.dss")

with phl.open("example.dss") as dss_file:    # closed for you at the end of the block
    ...

docs.title: DssFile
docs.text: An open DSS file. Create it with phl.open. It works as a context manager, so you can use it in a with block.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Name Type Description filename str path of the file is_open bool True until the file is closed

docs.title: write
docs.text:
dss_file.write(record) -> None

Saves a record to the file. record is a RegularTs, IrregularTs, PairedData or GriddedData.

Existing data at the same pathname is replaced:

  • time series: only the values inside the time span of the new record
  • paired and gridded data: the whole record

Raises TypeError for an unknown record type and IOError if HEC-DSS cannot write it.

docs.title: read
docs.text:
dss_file.read(path, start=None, end=None) -> RegularTs | IrregularTs | PairedData | GriddedData

Loads a record. The kind of record you get back depends on what is stored at path.

Parameter Type Description path str or DssPath pathname of the record start str, datetime or None time series only: start of the time window end str, datetime or None time series only: end of the time window

For a time series, an empty D part reads the whole series. Give both start and end to read only part of it. Raises KeyError if the record does not exist.

docs.title: catalog
docs.text:
dss_file.catalog(path_filter="", condensed=False, with_types=False) -> list

Lists the records in the file as a list of DssPath.

Parameter Type Description path_filter str only list matching pathnames, * matches many values condensed bool list each time series once, with its date range in the D part (like 01JAN2020-01MAR2020) instead of once per block with_types bool return (DssPath, record type code) pairs

A condensed pathname can be passed to read, find and delete.

docs.title: find
docs.text:
dss_file.find(path) -> list[DssPath]

Returns the pathnames of stored records that match path.

  • * at the start or end of a part matches many values, like /A/*/FLOW/*/*/*/ or /A/B/FL*/*/*/*/.
  • A time series pathname with an empty D part matches every block of that series.
  • A date range in the D part, like 01JAN2020-01MAR2020, matches the blocks inside that range.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
dss_file.delete(path) -> list[DssPath]

Deletes every record that matches path (same matching rules as find) and returns the pathnames it deleted. Raises KeyError if nothing matches.

docs.title: record_type
docs.text:
dss_file.record_type(path) -> int

Returns the HEC-DSS record type code of a record. Raises KeyError if the record does not exist.

Code Record type 105 regular time series 115 irregular time series 205 paired data 4xx gridded data (420, 430 and so on, by grid type)

docs.title: version
docs.text:
dss_file.version() -> int

Returns the DSS file version. Always 7.

docs.title: close
docs.text:
dss_file.close() -> None

Closes the file. A with block calls this for you.

docs.title: Records
docs.text: Records are plain Python objects. Create one, then save it with write. read gives you the same kind of object back. You can also read and change every field directly, like record.unit or record.values.

docs.title: RegularTs
docs.text:
phl.RegularTs(path, values, start, unit="", type="INST-VAL", time_zone="", save_as_float=False)

A time series with one value per fixed time step. The E part of the pathname sets the time step. Only the HEC-DSS standard intervals are accepted, any other E part raises ValueError:

  • 1SECOND, 2SECOND, 3SECOND, 4SECOND, 5SECOND, 6SECOND, 10SECOND, 15SECOND, 20SECOND, 30SECOND
  • 1MINUTE, 2MINUTE, 3MINUTE, 4MINUTE, 5MINUTE, 6MINUTE, 10MINUTE, 12MINUTE, 15MINUTE, 20MINUTE, 30MINUTE
  • 1HOUR, 2HOUR, 3HOUR, 4HOUR, 6HOUR, 8HOUR, 12HOUR
  • 1DAY, 1WEEK, SEMI-MONTH (periods start on the 1st and 16th), TRI-MONTH (1st, 11th and 21st), 1MONTH, 1YEAR
Parameter Type Description path str or DssPath pathname, like /BASIN/GAGE/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/ values list or 1d array the values, NaN for missing start str or datetime time of the first value unit str unit, like CFS type str data type, see data types time_zone str time zone name, like UTC save_as_float bool store as 32 bit floats to save space Attribute or method Description interval the time step, taken from the E part times pandas DatetimeIndex with the time of each value quality quality flags as a numpy array, only when read and present in the file to_series() returns a pandas Series indexed by time RegularTs.from_series(path, series, unit="", type="INST-VAL", **options) creates a record from a pandas Series with evenly spaced times

Monthly and yearly values that cover a whole period are stamped at the start of the next period. For example, the January 2020 value is at 01FEB2020 00:00.

docs.title: IrregularTs
docs.text:
phl.IrregularTs(path, times, values, unit="", type="INST-VAL", time_zone="", save_as_float=False)

A time series with values at any times. The E part starts with IR- or ~ and sets the storage block size, like IR-DAY, IR-MONTH or IR-YEAR.

Parameter Type Description path str or DssPath pathname, like /BASIN/GAGE/STAGE//IR-MONTH/OBS/ times list of times or DatetimeIndex time of each value, sorted and unique values list or 1d array the values, NaN for missing unit, type, time_zone, save_as_float same as RegularTs

Times are stored to the second. Raises ValueError if times and values have different lengths, or if the times are not sorted and unique.

Attribute or method Description quality quality flags as a numpy array, only when read and present in the file to_series() returns a pandas Series indexed by time IrregularTs.from_series(path, series, unit="", type="INST-VAL", **options) creates a record from a pandas Series with a time index

docs.title: PairedData
docs.text:
phl.PairedData(path, x, y, x_unit="", y_unit="", x_type="Linear", y_type="Linear", labels=[], time_zone="")

One or more curves that share the same x values, like a rating table.

Parameter Type Description path str or DssPath pathname, like /BASIN/GAGE/STAGE-FLOW///RATING/ x list or 1d array x values, shared by all curves y 1d or 2d array y values, shape [number of curves, number of points]. A 1d array is one curve. x_unit, y_unit str units of x and y x_type, y_type str axis type, like Linear or Log labels list of str a name for each curve, optional time_zone str time zone name

Raises ValueError if y does not match the length of x, or if the number of labels does not match the number of curves.

Attribute or method Description n_curves number of curves to_dataframe() returns a pandas DataFrame with x as the index and one column per curve PairedData.from_dataframe(path, df, x_unit="", y_unit="", **options) creates a record from a DataFrame. The index is x, each column is a curve, column names become labels.

docs.title: GriddedData
docs.text:
phl.GriddedData(path, data, cell_size, xll, yll, unit="", type="INST-VAL", grid_type="SPECIFIED",
                srs_wkt="", srs_name="", origin=(0, 0), data_source="", time_zone="")

A raster, like a radar rainfall grid or a DEM. The D and E parts are the start and end time, like 15JAN2020:0000. Leave both empty for a grid that does not change over time.

Parameter Type Description path str or DssPath pathname, like /SHG/BASIN/PRECIP/15JAN2020:0000/15JAN2020:0600/RADAR/ data 2d array grid values with shape [rows, columns]. The first row is the northern most. NaN means no data. Stored as float32. cell_size float width and height of a cell xll, yll float x and y of the lower left corner of the grid unit str unit, like MM type str data type, see data types grid_type str UNDEFINED, HRAP, ALBERS or SPECIFIED srs_wkt str coordinate system as WKT text srs_name str coordinate system name, like SHG origin (x, y) origin of the grid system. xll and yll must be a whole number of cells away from it. data_source str where the data came from time_zone str time zone name, like UTC

Raises ValueError if data is not a non empty 2d array, cell_size is not positive, grid_type is unknown, or the corner does not line up with origin.

Attribute Description shape (rows, columns) of the grid extent (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax), handy for matplotlib.pyplot.imshow(g.data, extent=g.extent) lower_left_cell (x, y) cell index of the lower left cell, counted in cells from origin start_time D part of the pathname, or None end_time E part of the pathname, or None

docs.title: DssPath
docs.text:
phl.DssPath(path)
phl.DssPath.from_parts(A="", B="", C="", D="", E="", F="")

A DSS pathname, /A/B/C/D/E/F/, split into its six parts. Every function that takes a pathname accepts a DssPath or a plain string, and catalog, find and delete return DssPath objects.

A DssPath cannot be changed. Use replace to get a new one. Two pathnames are equal when they match without looking at upper or lower case, and a DssPath can be compared with a string.

Raises ValueError if the pathname does not have six parts, is longer than 393 characters, or has a part longer than 64 characters.

Attribute or method Description A, B, C, D, E, F the parts as strings parts() the parts as a dict, {"A": ..., "F": ...} replace(**parts) a new pathname with some parts changed, like path.replace(F="SIM") without_date() a new pathname with an empty D part, which means the whole time series from_parts(A=..., F=...) builds a pathname from parts, missing parts are empty str(path) the pathname as a string 
path = phl.DssPath("/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW/01JAN2020/1HOUR/OBS/")
path.C                    # 'FLOW'
path.replace(F="SIM")     # DssPath('/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW/01JAN2020/1HOUR/SIM/')
path.without_date()       # DssPath('/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/')

docs.title: set_message_level
docs.text:
phl.set_message_level(level) -> int

Sets how many log messages the HEC-DSS library prints, from 0 (nothing) to 15 (everything). 1 prints only critical errors, 3 gives general information. Returns 0 on success.

When pyheclib is imported, the level is set from message_level_from_env.

docs.title: message_level_from_env
docs.text:
phl.message_level_from_env() -> int

Reads the DSS_MESSAGE_LEVEL environment variable. Returns its value if it is a whole number from 0 to 15, otherwise returns 1.

DSS_MESSAGE_LEVEL=3 python my_script.py

docs.title: api_version
docs.text:
phl.api_version() -> str

Returns the version of the bundled HEC-DSS C library API, like 0.3.0.

docs.title: __version__
docs.text: phl.__version__ is the pyheclib version, like 0.4.1.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
The type option of time series and gridded records is one of:

Type Meaning INST-VAL instant value at that time, like stage or flow INST-CUM running total at that time, like a rain gage counter PER-AVER average over the period ending at that time PER-CUM total over the period ending at that time, like hourly rainfall FREQ frequency value

docs.title: Other rules
docs.text:
• Missing values are NaN in every record type.
  • Regular time series: the E part sets the time step and must be a standard interval. Irregular: the E part starts with IR- or ~.
  • Leave the D part empty to read a whole time series. Use start and end for part of it.
  • Quality flags are read when present, but not written.

docs.title: Open and close a file
docs.text:
import pyheclib as phl

dss_file = phl.open("example.dss")   # opens the file, or creates it if it does not exist
# ... read and write records ...
dss_file.close()

You can also use with. The file is closed for you at the end of the block:

with phl.open("example.dss") as dss_file:
    print(dss_file.catalog())

docs.title: How records work
docs.text:
Every record is a Python object. It holds the pathname, the data and the metadata (units, data type and so on). The steps are always the same:

  1. Create a record object.
  2. Save it with dss_file.write(record).
  3. Load it with dss_file.read(pathname). You get back the same kind of object.
  4. Remove it with dss_file.delete(pathname).

Writing to a pathname that already has data replaces that data.

docs.title: Pathnames
docs.text:
Each record is stored under a pathname with six parts: /A/B/C/D/E/F/.

Part Usual meaning Example A project or basin DEMO B location OUTLET C parameter FLOW D start date or time 01JAN2020 E interval or end time 1HOUR F version or source OBS

DssPath helps you work with the parts. Anywhere a pathname is needed you can pass a DssPath or a plain string.

path = phl.DssPath("/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW/01JAN2020/1HOUR/OBS/")
path.C                        # 'FLOW'
path.replace(F="SIM")         # DssPath('/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW/01JAN2020/1HOUR/SIM/')
path.without_date()           # DssPath('/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/')
phl.DssPath.from_parts(A="DEMO", C="STAGE-FLOW", F="RATING")

docs.title: List the records in a file
docs.text:
dss_file = phl.open("example.dss")
dss_file.catalog()                                  # every record
dss_file.catalog(condensed=True)                    # one line per time series
dss_file.catalog("/DEMO/*/FLOW/*/*/*/")             # only matching records
dss_file.catalog(condensed=True, with_types=True)   # (path, record type code) pairs

DSS stores a long time series in blocks, for example one block per month for hourly data. catalog() shows every block. catalog(condensed=True) shows each time series once, with the D part set to its date range, like 01JAN2020-01MAR2020.

docs.title: Find records
docs.text:
find returns the pathnames that match. Put * at the start or end of any part to match many values.

dss_file.find("/DEMO/*/*/*/*/OBS/")      # every OBS record in DEMO
dss_file.find("/*/*/STAGE*/*/*/*/")      # STAGE and STAGE-FLOW records

docs.title: Delete records
docs.text:
delete removes every record that matches, and returns the pathnames it removed. It raises KeyError if nothing matches. Each record type page shows a delete example.

dss_file.delete("/SHG/*/*/*/*/*/")       # everything with A part SHG
dss_file.close()

docs.title: Missing values
docs.text: Missing values are NaN in every record type. pyheclib converts them to and from the DSS missing value for you.

docs.title: Log messages
docs.text:
The HEC-DSS library can print log messages. Set how much it prints with the DSS_MESSAGE_LEVEL environment variable before you import pyheclib:

export DSS_MESSAGE_LEVEL=3     # 0 prints nothing, 15 prints everything

If the variable is not set, or is not a whole number from 0 to 15, pyheclib uses 1, which prints only critical errors. You can also change it at any time in Python:

phl.set_message_level(3)

docs.title: Gridded data
docs.text: Gridded data stores a raster, like a radar rainfall grid or a DEM. In pyheclib it is a GriddedData record, and the data is a 2d numpy array.

docs.title: Pathname
docs.text:
The D and E parts are the start and end time of the grid, like 15JAN2020:0000 and 15JAN2020:0600. For a grid that does not change over time, like a DEM, leave both empty.

/SHG/DEMO/PRECIP/15JAN2020:0000/15JAN2020:0600/RADAR/
/SHG/DEMO/ELEVATION///DEM/

docs.title: The data array
docs.text:
• data is a 2d numpy array with shape [rows, columns].
  • The first row is the northern most row (north up), the same as most image formats.
  • NaN means no data.
  • Values are stored as 32 bit floats (float32).

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pyheclib as phl

dss_file = phl.open("example.dss")

yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:90, 0:140]
rain = (38*np.exp(-(((xx - 85)/22.0)**2 + ((yy - 40)/14.0)**2))).astype(np.float32)
rain[((xx - 70)/68.0)**2 + ((yy - 45)/44.0)**2 > 1] = np.nan     # outside the basin

grid = phl.GriddedData("/SHG/DEMO/PRECIP/15JAN2020:0000/15JAN2020:0600/RADAR/", rain,
                       cell_size=2000.0, xll=-180000.0, yll=1320000.0,
                       unit="MM", type="PER-CUM",
                       grid_type="ALBERS", srs_name="SHG", time_zone="UTC")
dss_file.write(grid)

xll and yll are the x and y of the lower left corner of the grid, in the grid's coordinate system. They must be a whole number of cells away from origin (default (0, 0)).

Writing replaces the whole record.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
g = dss_file.read("/SHG/DEMO/PRECIP/15JAN2020:0000/15JAN2020:0600/RADAR/")   # GriddedData
g.data              # 2d numpy array, NaN is no data
g.shape             # (rows, columns)
g.cell_size         # 2000.0
g.extent            # (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
g.lower_left_cell   # lower left cell index from origin
g.start_time, g.end_time

To plot it with matplotlib:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.imshow(g.data, extent=g.extent)
plt.colorbar(label=g.unit)
plt.show()

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
One grid:

dss_file.delete("/SHG/DEMO/PRECIP/15JAN2020:0000/15JAN2020:0600/RADAR/")

Or every grid of a parameter at once, using * in the D and E parts:

dss_file.delete("/SHG/DEMO/PRECIP/*/*/RADAR/")

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning cell_size required cell width and height xll, yll required lower left corner of the grid unit "" unit of the values, like MM type "INST-VAL" INST-VAL, INST-CUM, PER-AVER, PER-CUM or FREQ grid_type "SPECIFIED" UNDEFINED, HRAP, ALBERS or SPECIFIED srs_name "" name of the coordinate system, like SHG srs_wkt "" coordinate system as WKT text origin (0, 0) origin of the grid system data_source "" where the data came from time_zone "" time zone name, like UTC

docs.title: Irregular time series
docs.text: An irregular time series has values at any times, like manual stage readings. In pyheclib it is an IrregularTs record.

docs.title: Pathname
docs.text:
The E part starts with IR- (or ~) and sets the block size used for storage, for example IR-DAY, IR-MONTH or IR-YEAR. Pick a block size that holds a sensible number of values. Leave the D part empty.

/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE//IR-MONTH/OBS/

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
From times and values:

import pandas as pd
import pyheclib as phl

dss_file = phl.open("example.dss")

stage = phl.IrregularTs("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE//IR-MONTH/OBS/",
                        times=pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-14 08:13:00",
                                              "2020-01-15 07:30:15",
                                              "2020-01-16 16:45:00"]),
                        values=[3.1, 4.6, 3.4], unit="FT", type="INST-VAL")
dss_file.write(stage)

From a pandas Series with a time index:

series = pd.Series([3.1, 4.6, 3.4], index=pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-14 08:13",
                                                           "2020-01-15 07:30",
                                                           "2020-01-16 16:45"]))
dss_file.write(phl.IrregularTs.from_series("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE//IR-MONTH/OBS/", series, unit="FT"))

Times are stored to the second. Writing replaces stored values inside the time span of the new record. Values outside that span are kept.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
its = dss_file.read("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE//IR-MONTH/OBS/")   # IrregularTs
its.times         # pandas DatetimeIndex
its.values        # numpy array
its.to_series()   # pandas Series

Read only a time window with start and end:

its = dss_file.read("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE//IR-MONTH/OBS/", start="2020-01-15", end="2020-01-16")

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
An empty D part deletes the whole series:

dss_file.delete("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE//IR-MONTH/OBS/")

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning unit "" unit of the values, like FT type "INST-VAL" INST-VAL, INST-CUM, PER-AVER, PER-CUM or FREQ time_zone "" time zone name, like UTC save_as_float False store values as 32 bit floats to save space

docs.title: Paired data
docs.text: Paired data stores one or more curves that share the same x values, like a stage-flow rating table or an elevation-storage table. In pyheclib it is a PairedData record.

docs.title: Pathname
docs.text:
Paired data has no dates, so the D and E parts are usually empty. The C part names both parameters, like STAGE-FLOW.

/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE-FLOW///RATING/

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
x is a 1d array. y has one row per curve, so its shape is [number of curves, number of points]. labels gives each curve a name and is optional.

import numpy as np
import pyheclib as phl

dss_file = phl.open("example.dss")

stage = np.linspace(0, 12, 49)
rating = phl.PairedData("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE-FLOW///RATING/",
                        x=stage,
                        y=np.vstack([5.2*stage**1.80, 5.6*stage**1.75, 6.1*stage**1.70]),
                        x_unit="FT", y_unit="CFS", labels=["2018", "2019", "2020"])
dss_file.write(rating)

For a single curve, y can be a 1d array.

From a pandas DataFrame, where the index is x and each column is a curve:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"2020": 6.1*stage**1.70}, index=stage)
dss_file.write(phl.PairedData.from_dataframe("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE-FLOW///RATING/", df,
                                             x_unit="FT", y_unit="CFS"))

Writing replaces the whole record.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
rec = dss_file.read("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE-FLOW///RATING/")   # PairedData
rec.x, rec.y          # numpy arrays
rec.n_curves          # 3
rec.labels            # ['2018', '2019', '2020']
df = rec.to_dataframe()   # index is x, one column per curve

docs.title: Delete
docs.text: dss_file.delete("/DEMO/OUTLET/STAGE-FLOW///RATING/")

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning x_unit, y_unit "" units of x and y x_type, y_type "Linear" axis type, like Linear or Log labels [] one name per curve time_zone "" time zone name

docs.title: Regular time series
docs.text: A regular time series has one value per fixed time step, like hourly flow or daily rainfall. In pyheclib it is a RegularTs record.

docs.title: Pathname
docs.text:
The E part sets the time step. Common values are 15MINUTE, 1HOUR, 6HOUR, 1DAY, 1MONTH and 1YEAR. Leave the D part empty, pyheclib fills in the dates.

/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
From a list of values and the time of the first value:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyheclib as phl

dss_file = phl.open("example.dss")

precip = phl.RegularTs("/DEMO/GAGE/PRECIP//1DAY/OBS/",
                       values=[0.0, 12.5, 48.0, 3.1, 0.0],
                       start="2020-01-14", unit="MM", type="PER-CUM")
dss_file.write(precip)

From a pandas Series with a time index:

hours = pd.date_range("2020-01-14 01:00", periods=24*60, freq="h")   # 60 days of hourly data
flow = pd.Series(np.linspace(40, 90, hours.size), index=hours)
flow.iloc[70:76] = np.nan                     # missing values

record = phl.RegularTs.from_series("/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/", flow,
                                   unit="CFS", type="INST-VAL")
dss_file.write(record)

Writing replaces stored values inside the time span of the new record. Values outside that span are kept.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
Read the whole series:

rts = dss_file.read("/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/")    # RegularTs
rts.values        # numpy array
rts.times         # pandas DatetimeIndex
rts.start, rts.interval, rts.unit, rts.type
series = rts.to_series()                               # pandas Series

Read only a time window with start and end:

window = dss_file.read("/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/",
                       start="2020-01-15 12:00", end="2020-01-15 18:00")

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
To delete only some blocks, give a date range in the D part. DSS stores a long series in blocks (for hourly data, one block per month), and this removes the blocks in that range, not single values. catalog(condensed=True) shows the date range of each series.

dss_file.delete("/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW/01JAN2020-31JAN2020/1HOUR/OBS/")   # the January 2020 block

A pathname with an empty D part deletes the whole series, all blocks:

dss_file.delete("/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/")

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning unit "" unit of the values, like CFS or MM type "INST-VAL" INST-VAL, INST-CUM, PER-AVER, PER-CUM or FREQ time_zone "" time zone name, like UTC save_as_float False store values as 32 bit floats to save space

Note

Monthly and yearly values that cover a whole period are stamped at the start of the next period. For example, the January 2020 value is at 01FEB2020 00:00.

docs.title: Command line tools
docs.text: Installing pyheclib adds these commands on Linux, macOS and Windows. They live in pyheclib/tools and also run as python -m pyheclib.tools.<name>, for example from a clone with the extension built in place.

docs.title: List records: dss_catalog
docs.text:
Prints every record in a file with its record type code.

dss_catalog example.dss

Show each time series once instead of once per block:

dss_catalog example.dss --condensed

Show only matching records (use * in any part):

dss_catalog example.dss "/DEMO/*/FLOW/*/*/*/"

Record type codes:

Code Record type 105 regular time series 115 irregular time series 205 paired data 4xx gridded data (420, 421 and so on, by grid type)

docs.title: Export to CSV: dssrec2csv
docs.text:
Saves one record as a CSV file.

dssrec2csv example.dss "/DEMO/OUTLET/FLOW//1HOUR/OBS/" flow.csv
  • Time series: one row per time, with the time and the value.
  • Paired data: x in the first column, one column per curve.
  • Gridded data: the grid as rows and columns, north at the top.

For a time series, leave the D part empty to export the whole series.

docs.title: Example files
docs.text:
The repository also has scripts that create example data:

python3 examples/make_example_dss.py       # builds examples/example.dss with every record type
python3 examples/make_readme_figures.py    # draws the figures used in these docs

docs.title: DSS viewer
docs.text: The DSS viewer lets you look inside DSS files in your web browser. It runs on your own computer and needs nothing besides pyheclib.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
The viewer comes with pyheclib as the dss_browser command:

pip install pyheclib

It is a single script, pyheclib/tools/dss_browser.py, and also runs as python -m pyheclib.tools.dss_browser.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
dss_browser example.dss

The viewer opens in your web browser at http://127.0.0.1:8765/. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.

You can open more than one file:

dss_browser basin.dss radar.dss

Options:

Option Default Meaning --port 8765 port to serve on --host 127.0.0.1 address to serve on --no-browser off do not open the web browser for you

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
• Open files: use the Open button, or drag .dss files onto the page. Each file gets its own tab.
  • Find records: type in the search box. Every word must match.
    • A plain word matches anywhere in the pathname, like FLOW or /OUTLET/FLOW/.
    • B=GAGE finds GAGE anywhere in part B. Add * or ? to match the whole part instead, like C=FLOW* (FLOW, FLOW-PEAK but not STAGE-FLOW).
    • The type menu shows only one record type, like regular time series or grids.
  • View a record: click a record to see its metadata and simple statistics. Switch between Graph (a chart, or an image for grids) and Table to see the data.
  • Download: click Download CSV to save the record as a CSV file.
  • Share a link: each record has its own address, like /?file=1&path=/A/B/C/D/E/F/.
  • Light or dark: the button at the top right switches the theme. Your choice is remembered.
  • Resize: drag the line between the record list and the record to change their widths.

Time series are listed once each, with their full date range, instead of once per block.

If you stop the server, the page fades out. It reconnects when the server starts again.

docs.title: Try it with the example file
docs.text:
The repository has an example file with every record type:

dss_browser examples/example.dss
